content:
In the past couple of days, two reports have suggested ways Apple could increase its services revenue to boost profits.

In my view, Apple should absolutely do the first thing, but not the second — and it looks like Phil Schiller might agree…

Let me first summarize the two reports.

Home security and monitoring service

On Friday, a Bloomberg report said Apple may be planning to launch an entirely new home security and monitoring service, alongside some of the new home hardware we're expecting.

Squeezing more money from the App Store

A second Bloomberg report, published on Sunday, said Apple is looking at how to extract more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should not do the second one

Conversely, I think the second approach would be a huge mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly over the sale of iPhone apps is already under heavy fire from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell iPhone apps, you have to do so via the official App Store, leaving you with no choice but to accept Apple's take-it-or-leave-it terms.

I know a common view is that nobody is forcing you to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that's not how even the most laissez-faire form of capitalism works: the US has had antitrust laws since 1890. Once you achieve a certain level of market dominance, your behavior is constrained to ensure you don't abuse that position.

Trying to squeeze more money from the App Store is entirely skating away from where the puck is heading, and Phil Schiller is reportedly of the same view — which Bloomberg says is one of the reasons for his stepping back now.

Innovative services are the way to go

Launching innovative services that consumers choose to buy, by contrast, is absolutely the right direction for Apple. I can easily see the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

Back in 2024, I said making its own smart home cameras would be one of the smartest things the company could do. I said the same about rumored Apple smart doorbells. Offering an optional service tie-in for security products makes complete sense, for two reasons.

First, for all the privacy reasons I've previously outlined. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal to ensure the privacy of security camera footage. If there's one company I'd trust to perform AI analysis of security camera video, it's Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate the security hardware and service within the HomeKit environment. I'm sure there are many other areas where Apple could play a similar role.

For me, the key thing is that Apple needs to treat services with the same approach it takes to hardware. Make great products that people willingly and happily pay for. Not extract money in a way that annoys consumers, developers, and regulators.

What do you think? Please share your views in the comments.
